So the scribes are not being obtuse. They have correctly identified that the man in the room has done something only the God of Israel does, and they draw the only conclusion their categories allow. Mark lets their logic stand unchallenged, because he intends the reader to run it to the end: if the premise is true and Jesus is not blaspheming, there is exactly one thing left that he can be.

Note also where the forgiveness happens. Not in the temple, ninety miles south, through a priest and a lamb. On earth (v. 10) — in a crowded fishing-village house, from the mouth of a carpenter, to a man who had not brought a sacrifice.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: four men digging through someone else's roof because the door was blocked by people who had come to hear Jesus. The obstacle was not his enemies; it was the crowd around him.

Now: the friend or parent who keeps carrying a name to God when the person attached to it will not come — who has been carrying it for years, and has watched the door stay shut. Mark records that Jesus saw their faith, and did not ask the man on the mat for a statement first.

There is a warning folded into the same scene. The people blocking the door were not opponents. They were admirers who had got there early and would not move. It is possible to be so close to Jesus, and so pleased to be close, that you become the reason somebody else cannot reach him. The four went over the top of that crowd, and the crowd got a shower of dried mud for its trouble.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he returned to Capernaum after some days, it was reported that he was at home. And many were gathered together, so that there was no more room, not even at the door. And he was preaching the word to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Picture the house. Capernaum was a fishing village of maybe fifteen hundred people on the north shore of the lake, and the houses were single-storey, built of black basalt field-stone laid up without mortar, roofed with beams and branches and packed mud. A family room was perhaps eighteen feet square. Archaeologists have dug up a house there, a few steps from the synagogue, that was venerated as Peter's by Christians within a couple of generations. That is almost certainly the address Mark means when he writes, with no ceremony at all, that he was at home.

The Son of God, in this Gospel, does not have a headquarters. He has a friend's spare room.

After some days. Mark has just told us why there was a gap. At the end of chapter 1 the healed leper published the news so widely that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town, but was out in desolate places (1:45). He had been driven into the countryside by his own success. Coming back to Capernaum was a calculated return, and the town found out in hours.

No more room, not even at the door. Count what that means physically. The room is full and standing; the doorway is packed; the courtyard beyond it is packed; there are people in the street craning at a window slot. This is why the four could not get near, and it is worth being honest about who was in the way. Not the authorities. Not enemies. People who had come to hear Jesus, had arrived first, and were not moving.

And he was preaching the word to them. Mark saves this clause for last and most readers skip it. The crowd has come because of what happened in chapter 1 — a demon silenced, a fever broken, a leper touched. What Jesus is actually doing when they arrive is talking. The miracles were never the ministry; they were the credentials of the ministry.

Try the test on yourself, because it is the one the chapter is quietly running on the crowd. Suppose the healing you are waiting for never comes, and what remains is a Person who speaks and asks to be believed. Would you still have made the walk to the door? The crowd in this room was never asked that question directly. You are being asked it now, and your answer will decide whether the rest of the chapter is good news or merely impressive.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came, bringing to him a paralytic carried by four men. And when they could not get near him because of the crowd, they removed the roof above him, and when they had made an opening, they let down the bed on which the paralytic lay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now watch four men do something that ought to have got them thrown out.

The roof of a Galilean house was not a structure you would trust a ladder to. Beams of sycamore or rough timber were laid across the walls; branches and reed matting were cross-laid over the beams; then a thick layer of mud mixed with straw was packed on top and rolled flat with a stone cylinder after the rains, which is why every house had one on the roof. An outside stair ran up the side wall, because the roof was usable space — you dried figs on it, you slept on it in summer. Getting a man up there on a mat was heavy, awkward work for four, but it was possible.

What they did next was not repair-able in an afternoon. Mark's verb is blunt: they dug out the roof. Mud, straw, matting, branches, all of it coming down in a shower on the heads of a packed room, with the preacher underneath. Luke, writing for readers who lived in tiled Greek cities, translates the scene into tiles; Mark, closer to the ground, gives you the dirt.

The bed. The word Mark uses is krabattos — not a bed frame but a poor man's pallet, a mat you could roll and carry. It is a rough, colloquial Latin loan-word, one of a string of Latinisms in this Gospel that suggest Mark was writing for Romans. The man's whole world was a piece of quilted matting and four friends.

Carried by four men. They are never named. They say nothing in the entire episode. They do not appear again in Scripture. Their entire recorded contribution to the kingdom of God is that they would not accept a locked door.

And notice whose house it was. If this is Peter's house, then somebody who had just left his nets to follow Jesus watched his own ceiling come down into his own front room, and Mark records not one word of complaint from anybody. There was a man outside who needed to get in. The roof was only a roof.

It is worth asking what you would let be damaged — your dignity, your schedule, your carefully managed reputation as a reasonable person — to get one man in front of Christ. These four are in the Bible forever because they were willing to make a mess.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, "Son, your sins are forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when Jesus saw their faith.

Their faith. Not his. Mark does not tell us one thing about what the man on the mat believed — whether he had asked to be brought, whether he was ashamed to be lowered into a crowded room in front of the whole village, whether he expected anything at all. What Jesus saw and honoured was the faith of the men on the roof.

That single word carries a question a great many readers bring to this passage with a particular face in mind: a child who has walked away, a husband who will not believe, a friend long past caring. Can my faith do for them what these four did for their friend? The answer is yes and no, and both halves matter.

Yes. Your faith can carry a person to the place where Jesus is, and that is precisely what intercession does. You cannot make anyone believe, but you can bring them, again and again, into the presence of the one who can: under the preached word, onto your prayer list, into the company of his people. You can refuse, as these men refused, to accept that the door is shut and the case is closed.

And no. Notice that the man did not stay a spectator of his own healing. He heard your sins are forgiven; he rose and walked. No one was forgiven in his place and no one repented for him. You cannot believe in another's stead; each must finally meet Christ himself. So your part is the roof and the ropes — getting them where grace is found; the rising is God's to give and theirs to receive. Many a believer walking with Christ today was once only a name on somebody's stubborn, seemingly unanswered prayer list. Do not stop digging through the roof.

Son. The word is teknon, child — a warm, domestic word, the word a father uses. The man has been lowered into a room full of strangers and religious professionals, filthy from the ceiling, at the centre of everyone's attention, and the first word spoken to him is a family word. Before anything is said about his sins or his legs, he is told where he stands.

Your sins are forgiven. Why this, and not the legs, when the legs are what everyone in the room is looking at?

Not, most likely, because the paralysis was a punishment for some particular sin. Scripture is careful here. Sometimes suffering is tied to a specific sin — sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you (John 5:14). Very often it is not at all — neither this man nor his parents sinned (John 9:3). The point is simpler and deeper than cause and effect. The four friends and the whole crowd could see a ruined body. Jesus saw the ruined man, and went first to his greatest need.

Hold the two outcomes side by side and the priority stops being abstract. A paralytic who walked home that afternoon and died unforgiven forty years later would still be lost. A paralytic forgiven and never healed, carried on that mat to the end of his life, would be eternally safe. Jesus heals the legs to prove that he has dealt with the soul — but he leaves nobody in the room in any doubt about which was the emergency. He gives the lesser gift as the visible receipt for the greater one.

And there is the mercy of it. He begins where you would not have begun, with the thing you were not asking about, because he is treating you as a man and not as a case.

verseByVerse.quote: Now some of the scribes were sitting there, questioning in their hearts, "Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nobody has said a word. Mark tells us that some of the scribes were sitting there — seated, which in that culture is the posture of the qualified man, the one who has come to assess rather than to listen — questioning in their hearts. The whole exchange that follows begins as an argument that never got said out loud.

And their theology is exactly right. This is the thing to get hold of before anything else: the scribes in this room are not fools and they are not straw men. They know their Bible.

Who can forgive sins but God alone? That is not prejudice; it is Isaiah. I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake (Isa. 43:25) — and the doubled pronoun is the whole force of it. Pardon is God's own act. A priest could declare a healed leper clean. A prophet could announce that God had forgiven. A rabbi could teach the road back. Not one of them ever stood in front of a man and forgave him, because the offence in every sin is finally against God, and only the one offended can wipe the account. David understood this with a murdered man's blood on his hands: Against you, you only, have I sinned (Ps. 51:4).

Nor was this something anyone expected the Messiah to do. Israel's hope was a king who would reign, drive out the Romans, and rule the nations. No Jewish writing before Jesus has the Messiah pronouncing forgiveness in his own name. This is not a Messianic claim being made too loudly. It is a category the Messianic hope did not contain.

He is blaspheming. Fix the word in your mind, because it is a death sentence and it lands in chapter 2. Leviticus 24:16 prescribes stoning for it. When Mark reaches the night trial, the high priest tears his robe and says You have heard his blasphemy, and they all condemn him as deserving death (14:64). The verdict that kills Jesus is reached, silently, in a crowded front room in Capernaum, twelve chapters before it is carried out. Everything in between is the trial.

Now run the scribes' logic honestly, because Mark wants you to. Their major premise is true: only God forgives sins. Their minor premise is true: this man just forgave sins. There is no third conclusion available. Either he is a blasphemer of the first order, or he is what the voice at the Jordan called him. What is not available — what has never been available, whatever the century decides to say about him — is the comfortable middle position that he was a fine moral teacher who would be appalled at what his followers made of him. Fine moral teachers do not do this.

And here is the sting for religious people. The scribes were right about God and wrong about Jesus. They had the doctrine of divine pardon perfectly in place, and it was the very shelf on which they filed him as an enemy. It is entirely possible to hold every article of the faith correctly and be undone by the Person the articles are about — to know what only God can do, watch him do it, and conclude that he must be got rid of. Ask yourself, before you enjoy their mistake too much, whether your settled convictions about how God works have room in them for God turning up and working.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately Jesus, perceiving in his spirit that they thus questioned within themselves, said to them, "Why do you question these things in your hearts? Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, 'Your sins are forgiven,' or to say, 'Rise, take up your bed and walk'?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Jesus answers the objection he demonstrates something nobody in the room stops to comment on: he answers an objection that was never spoken. Mark says he was perceiving in his spirit that they thus questioned within themselves. The scribes have not moved a muscle. He reads the silence.

Solomon, dedicating the temple, prayed to the God who alone can do that: you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind (1 Kgs. 8:39). Jeremiah says the heart is deceitful above all things and desperately sick, and then asks who can understand it, and God answers: I the LORD search the heart (Jer. 17:9–10). So there are now two divine prerogatives exercised in ninety seconds — forgiving sin and reading the heart — and the men best equipped to notice are the ones being read.

Which is easier? Sit with the question, because it is not the trick it first appears. Easier to say. That is the exact wording, and it decides the whole argument.

Saying your sins are forgiven is the easy sentence, because nothing in the visible world changes when you say it. There is no test. A charlatan could say it in every village in Galilee for a decade and never be caught, because the claim is unfalsifiable by design.

Saying rise, take up your bed and walk is the hard sentence. It is checkable in about four seconds, in front of a packed room, and if the man does not move you are finished. Every religious fraud in history has instinctively preferred claims that cannot be tested.

So Jesus does the reverse of what a fraud does. He deliberately hangs the invisible claim on a visible, immediate, public, falsifiable test, and he tells the room in advance that this is what he is doing. He is not hiding behind mystery. He is inviting verification.

That instinct runs right through the faith, and it is worth a non-specialist knowing it. Paul does not tell the Corinthians to have a personal experience; he says that if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain and you are still in your sins (1 Cor. 15:14, 17), and then lists the surviving eyewitnesses and invites the reader to go and ask them. Christianity has always staked itself on things that could in principle be shown to be false.

Which raises a fair question to run on yourself. What would have to happen for you to conclude that what you believe is not true? If the honest answer is nothing at all — if no possible fact could touch it — then what you have may be a mood rather than a faith. Jesus did not ask this room to feel something about him. He asked it to watch, and to draw the conclusion the evidence required.

verseByVerse.quote: But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins"—he said to the paralytic— "I say to you, rise, pick up your bed, and go home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the sentence and notice that it breaks in half. Jesus is speaking to the scribes — that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins — and then, mid-argument, Mark inserts a stage direction: he turned and spoke to the paralytic. The dashes in your Bible are the translators marking the swivel. The theological point is aimed at the professionals; the command is aimed at the man on the floor. Jesus never finishes the sentence to the scribes. The finish is the man standing up.

On earth. Two small words, and they relocate the whole apparatus of pardon. Not in heaven, at some assize after you die, where you will find out how it went. Not ninety miles south in Jerusalem, through a priest and a lamb and a curtain and a fee. Here — on the ground, in a fishing village, in a room with mud on the floor, from the mouth of a man you could touch, to somebody who had brought no sacrifice and could not have carried one if he had.

The Son of Man. This is the first time in Mark that Jesus names himself, and it is his settled way of speaking about himself all the way to the cross. In ordinary Aramaic the phrase could mean nothing more than a human being. But Jesus is reaching for something enormous. It comes from Daniel 7, where the prophet watches thrones being set in place and the Ancient of Days taking his seat — and then sees one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, presented before God, and given dominion and glory and a kingdom, so that all peoples and nations should serve him, an everlasting dominion that shall not pass away (Dan. 7:13–14).

Coming with the clouds is not incidental scenery. In the Old Testament the one who rides the clouds is God. Daniel sees a figure who is genuinely human and is given what belongs to God, and Jesus picks that figure up and puts it on. So when he says the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins — and again at the end of this chapter, that the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath — he is not claiming a right any man might have. He is claiming the authority Daniel saw handed to that heavenly Man.

The title is perfectly chosen. It is veiled enough that no one can convict him on it in a hurry, and plain enough that anyone with the Scriptures open can see what has been said. Before Mark is finished, this name will carry both his throne and his cross — for it is the Son of Man who came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45).

Rise, pick up your bed, and go home. Three commands, and the third is the tender one. He is not sent to the temple, or to a rabbi, or on a lap of the town to prove it. He is sent home, and somebody there — a wife, a mother, the children who had learned to step around a mat on the floor — is about to look up and see him standing in the doorway on his own legs, carrying the thing that carried him.

That is the shape of everything this Man does. He does not merely repair you and leave you standing in the road. He sends you home.

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and immediately picked up his bed and went out before them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying, "We never saw anything like this!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately. It is Mark's favourite word — he uses it more than forty times in sixteen chapters, and it gives the Gospel its breathless pace. Here it does real work. There is no convalescence, no gradual return of feeling, no weeks of learning to walk. The command and the walking are the same instant, because the authority behind the command is not the kind that has to wait for nature to catch up.

Before them all. The healing is not done quietly in a back room and reported afterwards. Jesus staked a claim on a public test, and the test is settled publicly, in front of the very scribes who had silently convicted him, with the crowd parting to let a man walk out through the door his friends could not get him through.

And there is a small human detail in that exit. He picked up his bed. He did not leave the mat lying there to be tidied away; he carried out the thing that had carried him in. What had been the emblem of his helplessness went home over his shoulder as evidence.

We never saw anything like this. Now weigh the crowd's verdict carefully, because Mark has put it there for weighing. They were amazed. They glorified God — which is right, and better than the scribes managed. But read what they say, and then read what they do not say.

Not one person in that room says: then the other thing he said must be true as well. Nobody asks the obvious follow-up question. Nobody says, if he can do that to a man's legs with a word, what has he just done to a man's guilt, and could he do it for me? They had been handed the proof, in the terms Jesus himself set, and their astonishment stopped at the miracle and never reached the thing the miracle was for.

That failure is not a first-century failure. It is entirely possible to be moved by the power of God and unmoved by the pardon of God — to want him for what he might fix and never once come to him for what he came to forgive. A great deal of modern praying is exactly this. We ask him about the legs. He is waiting to talk about the sins.

So run the honest inventory. Think of the last five things you asked God for. How many were about circumstances, and how many were about your soul? There is no shame in asking him for the legs; the four friends did, and he did not scold them. But if the whole list is legs, you have understood him about as well as the crowd did — and they went home amazed and unforgiven.

The man on the mat got both, and only one of them was still with him fifty years later.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — Levi, Sinners, and New Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Out again (vv. 13–14). Jesus leaves the house, teaches by the lake, and walks past a customs post. Sitting in it is Levi son of Alphaeus, a Jew collecting money for the occupying power, and the two words Follow me end his career in the time it takes to say them.

The dinner (vv. 15–17). Levi's first recorded act as a disciple is to throw a party for his own disreputable network and put Jesus at the centre of it. The scribes of the Pharisees do not challenge Jesus; they go at him through his followers. His answer is one sentence about a doctor, and it sorts the human race into two categories with no third.

The fasting question (vv. 18–20). Why do John's disciples fast and yours do not? Jesus answers with a wedding, quietly takes for himself a role the Old Testament gives to God alone, and in the same breath drops the first shadow of the cross into the Gospel.

Cloth and wineskins (vv. 21–22). Two pictures from ordinary domestic life make one uncomfortable point: what he has brought cannot be sewn onto what you already have.
verseByVerse.theology:
The two little parables of vv. 21–22 are the theological hinge of the chapter, and they are more radical than they look. An unshrunk patch on an old garment does not merely fail; when it is first washed it shrinks, grips, and pulls away, and the tear is worse than it was before the repair. New wine still working gives off gas; a skin that has already stretched once and gone brittle will split. In both pictures the old thing is not attacked. It is simply asked to contain something it was never built to hold, and it fails.

Jesus is not offering a reformed Judaism, and he is not offering a reformed you. Religion, as everyone naturally practises it, is patchwork — an addition to a self that stays fundamentally in charge. That, he says, does not produce a better garment; it produces a worse tear, which is exactly why adding a little Christianity to an unchanged life so often makes a person more miserable rather than less.

And then the promise at the end, which is easy to read past: new wine is for fresh wineskins. He supplies the skin as well as the wine. I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezek. 36:26); if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation (2 Cor. 5:17). He did not come to mend you. That is worse news, and far better news, than mending.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Levi cannot yet explain a doctrine, so he cooks. He gathers the only people he knows — the ones no synagogue wanted — and gets them into a room with Jesus.

Now: the newest Christian in your church, six weeks old in the faith, still knows every person from the old life; the man who has been converted thirty years often knows nobody outside the church at all. Levi's method needs no training course. Buy the food, make the call, and be in the room.

The harder half of the example is the one people skip. Jesus went to that table as the physician, not as a patient, and nobody left it unchanged — the meal ended with Levi following him, not with Jesus agreeing with the guests. Both errors are live. One keeps a safe distance and calls it holiness; the other sits down at every table, says nothing about Christ for fifteen years, and calls it grace. The Pharisees would not go in. Jesus went in, and went in as himself.

verseByVerse.quote: He went out again beside the sea, and all the crowd was coming to him, and he was teaching them. And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, "Follow me." And he rose and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went out again beside the sea. It is worth noticing how often Mark's Jesus leaves. He leaves the synagogue, the house, the crowd, the town. He has just performed the most spectacular thing yet seen in Capernaum, and his response to a full house is to go outside and walk along the shore.

And as he walks he passes a customs post, and the whole chapter turns.

Levi the son of Alphaeus. Matthew's Gospel calls the same man Matthew (Matt. 9:9), and it is a fair guess that Levi was the name he was born with and Matthew — which means gift of God — was the name he carried afterwards. Mark, writing about him in the third person, uses the old name. Matthew, writing about himself, uses the new one and adds the words the tax collector to his own name in the apostle list (Matt. 10:3), which nobody else does to him. A forgiven man is not embarrassed by his file.

Sitting at the tax booth. Capernaum sat on the road that ran from Damascus down to the Mediterranean, and it was a border town — the frontier of Herod Antipas's territory. A booth there was a licence to print money. Understand how the system worked and you understand the loathing: the collector bid for the contract, paid the authorities up front, and lived on whatever he could extract above that figure. There was no published rate a man could appeal to. Whatever he said you owed, backed by soldiers, is what you owed.

So a tax collector was two things at once, and both were unforgivable. He was a thief with legal cover, and he was a collaborator — a Jew making his living off the occupation of his own country. He could not give evidence in court, because his word was worth nothing. He was barred from the synagogue. Money from his hand could not be received.

And there was worse, which the crowd would have felt without needing it explained. The road back for a thief ran through restitution: you repaid what you took, and added a fifth (Num. 5:7; Lev. 6:5). A tax collector could not do it. He had defrauded hundreds of people over years and kept no list of who they were. His repentance was, in the judgement of his own religion, mathematically impossible. He was in a class of men widely regarded as beyond saving.

That is the man Jesus stops for.

Follow me. Two words in the Greek. No interview, no probation, no conditions, no requirement that he first put anything right. And Mark, who never wastes a syllable, gives the response in five: and he rose and followed him.

Weigh what that cost against what it cost the fishermen. Peter and Andrew left their nets, and the nets were still there — after the crucifixion they went straight back to them for a night (John 21:3). Levi stood up from a booth that somebody else would be sitting in by the afternoon. There was no going back to that job, ever, and everyone in Capernaum knew it. His was the one call in the Gospel that could not be reversed, and he made it without asking a single question.

If you have ever privately concluded that you have gone too far, been at it too long, done the kind of damage that cannot be undone or repaid — look hard at who is sitting in that booth. The man Jesus chose for the apostolic band, and for the writing of a Gospel, was the one man in town whose religion had already given up on him.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he reclined at table in his house, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many who followed him. And the scribes of the Pharisees, when they saw that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, said to his disciples, "Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Levi's first act as a disciple is to give a party. Luke tells us plainly that he made him a great feast in his house (Luke 5:29), and Mark's word for it is that they were reclining — not perched on stools grabbing a bite, but stretched out on couches around a low table in the posture of a formal banquet, which meant hours.

And the room was full of the only people Levi knew.

Tax collectors and sinners. The second word is not a general observation about human nature; it was a technical term. The sinners were those whose trade or way of life put them permanently outside the reach of the purity system — the collectors and their friends, and everyone the religious establishment had written off as unreachable. Mark adds a detail that is easy to miss: there were many who followed him. Levi's network was already moving.

Why this detonated. A modern reader has to be told this, because we eat with anybody. In that world a shared table was not a neutral social event. It was the sign of full acceptance — of peace between the people at it. You did not eat with a man you regarded as unclean, because you would be saying, in the most public way available, that there was nothing between you. That is precisely what Jesus was saying, and everybody in Capernaum could read it.

Said to his disciples. Note the tactic, because it is ancient and still in use. The scribes of the Pharisees do not put the question to Jesus. They take it to his followers, who are new, unsure of their ground, and much easier to unsettle. If you cannot get at the leader, get at the people who follow him and make them feel foolish about the company they are keeping.

Now the question this raises for anyone trying to live in two worlds at once. How do I keep real friendships with people whose lives I do not agree with, without either condemning them or quietly signing off on everything?

Jesus is the answer, and he gives it by being at the table rather than by drawing a line around it. But look closely at how he is there. He is not blending in and hoping not to be noticed. He is not there as a fellow patient. The evening ends with the host giving up his career, and it never once ends with Jesus agreeing with the room.

So here is a test you can actually run. Think of the last evening you spent among people far from God. Two questions, and answer them honestly. Did anything about the way you were there make Christ visible — or were you simply indistinguishable? And did you go home more like them, or did any of them go home having met something in you they could not account for?

Most of us fail this in one of two directions, and the church has a long history of both. The Pharisees would not go in at all and called it holiness. Others go in, sit down, say nothing about Christ for fifteen years, and call it grace. Jesus went in — and went in as himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus heard it, he said to them, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One sentence, and it is the whole gospel with the bark still on it.

Those who are well have no need of a physician. Do not miss the irony, because Jesus is not conceding the point. He is not agreeing that the Pharisees are spiritually healthy; he is taking their own self-assessment and following it to its end. Very well — if you are well, you will not want a doctor, and you will not get one. It is the gentlest and most terrible sentence in the chapter.

Because that is exactly how it works with actual medicine. The man who will not admit he is ill does not take the treatment. He does not need a rarer disease or a scarcer drug; the cure is on the shelf in the house. He dies of something treatable, holding the position that there is nothing wrong with him.

I came. It is the first time in Mark that Jesus speaks like this, and the words carry more than they seem to. Nobody says I came about being born. A man who says he came was somewhere before, and had business here.

Not to call the righteous, but sinners. The verb is the same one that landed on Levi at the booth three verses earlier. This is not theory; the room is the evidence.

And here is the thing that makes this good news rather than merely fair-minded: the only qualification for Christ is the disqualification. Not progress. Not a clean stretch. Not having got the worst of it behind you. Sickness is the entry requirement, and the ticket is the thing you have been trying to hide.

Which cuts two ways, and you should know which way it cuts for you.

If your fear is that you are too far gone — that if the people in your church knew what was actually in your history or your head, that would be the end of it — then read the sentence again slowly. He did not come for the respectable and take the odd sinner as an exception. He came for sinners. You are not the awkward case. You are the stated purpose of the visit.

But if your quiet position is that you are basically all right — decent, churchgoing, never did anybody much harm — then this verse is not a comfort, and it is not meant to be. There is no third category. There are the sick who know it, and the sick who do not, and only one of those groups ever sends for the doctor. The Pharisees went home from Levi's house that night with their theology intact, their reputations intact, and their sins intact.

Here is the test, and it takes about a minute. When did you last tell God something specific and shameful about yourself, in plain words, without softening it? Not a general admission that we all fall short — the actual thing. A man who cannot remember doing that is a man who has not yet gone to the physician, however long he has been sitting in the waiting room.

And consider what it cost the Physician to say it. Doctors keep their distance; they wash, they wear gloves, they go home. This one came into the ward, took the disease into his own body, and died of it, so that the patients would live. He was not being broad-minded at Levi's table. He was starting the treatment.

verseByVerse.quote: Now John's disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. And people came and said to him, "Why do John's disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast?" And Jesus said to them, "Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in that day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The question comes from an odd alliance. John's disciples were ascetics, formed by a man in camel's hair who lived on locusts. The Pharisees were the strictest religious party in the country. They agreed on almost nothing else, and they are united here in genuine bewilderment: everybody serious fasts. Why do yours not?

It was a fair question. The Law of Moses commanded exactly one fast in the year, on the Day of Atonement (Lev. 16:29). The Pharisees fasted twice a week — the man in Jesus's parable says so himself with some pride (Luke 18:12) — and by any measure of the day, a teacher whose followers did not fast was not a serious teacher.

Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? Jesus does not defend his disciples. He changes the category entirely, and he does it with a picture every person listening had stood inside.

A Jewish wedding ran seven days. The phrase behind wedding guests is literally the sons of the bridechamber — the groom's closest friends, the men who ran the celebration. And here is the edge of the answer: the rabbis themselves ruled that those men were released from certain religious obligations for the week, because you cannot mourn and rejoice at once. Jesus is answering out of their own law. Fasting at this moment would not be devotion. It would be a man sitting in the corner of a wedding feast, refusing the food, with the bridegroom in the room.

Then notice what he has just said about himself while apparently talking about lunch.

Who is the bridegroom? In the Old Testament that role belongs to one Person, and there is no second candidate. Your Maker is your husband, the LORD of hosts is his name (Isa. 54:5). As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you (Isa. 62:5). I will betroth you to me forever (Hos. 2:19). Jesus picks up the title and wears it without a word of explanation, in the middle of an answer about diet. It is the second enormous claim of the chapter, and unlike the first one, nobody in the room seems to have noticed.

And it tells you what he thinks his own presence is. Not an examination. Not an inspection. A wedding — the happiest week in a village's life, food and wine and noise and a groom who cannot stop smiling. That is his account of what it is like to be near him. If your religion feels nothing like that, it is worth asking whether you have understood who is in the room.

When the bridegroom is taken away. And then, in a single clause, the light goes out of the sentence. The verb is not gentle; it means to be taken away by force, snatched off. Bridegrooms are not removed from their own weddings. This is the first shadow of the cross in Mark's Gospel — dropped into a cheerful answer about fasting, in chapter 2, before any opponent has laid a finger on him. He knew, this early, how it ended.

Then they will fast in that day. Which settles the practical question a reader is entitled to ask: are Christians meant to fast now? Jesus plainly assumed so. He did not say fasting was abolished; he said its time was coming. And when he taught his disciples about it he never said if you fast but when you fast (Matt. 6:16–17), which is not the language of an optional extra for specialists.

What it is not is a way of getting God's attention or paying something off. What it is, is a way of making the body say what the heart means — of deliberately going hungry for a few hours so that a real, physical, insistent ache reminds you, every twenty minutes, that there is a deeper hunger you have been feeding with everything except God. The stomach becomes an alarm clock.

If you have never done it, start absurdly small. Miss one meal this week; do not tell anybody; spend the time you would have spent eating with the Bible open, and let the hunger do its work of reminding you what you actually want. You will learn more about your own heart in ninety minutes of that than in a month of reading about it.

And keep the order of the two halves. We fast because the Bridegroom has been taken away and we want him back. It is not gloom. It is homesickness with a date in it — for he was taken away on a Friday, and the wedding feast that all the others were rehearsing has been fixed for a day that has already been named (Rev. 19:9).

verseByVerse.quote: No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the patch tears away from it, the new from the old, and a worse tear is made. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins—and the wine is destroyed, and so are the skins. But new wine is for fresh wineskins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two pictures from ordinary domestic life, and both of them are about the same mistake.

The patch. New cloth off the loom is unshrunk. Sew a piece of it onto a garment that has already been washed a hundred times, and for a while it looks like a decent repair. Then it gets wet, and the new patch pulls tight while the worn cloth around it has no give left, and it rips away and takes the old fabric with it. Mark's summary is bleak and exact: a worse tear is made. The garment was damaged before. It is ruined now, and the repair did it.

The skin. Wine in that world was carried in whole goatskins. Fresh must is still fermenting; it gives off gas and swells hard against the container, which is why it went into a new skin with stretch left in it. An old skin has already done its stretching and has gone dry and brittle. Pour working wine into it and it splits — and Jesus makes a point of counting the cost twice: the wine is destroyed, and so are the skins. You do not merely fail to gain the new. You lose what you had.

Now hear what he is actually saying, because it is more radical than it sounds and it is aimed at a very ordinary way of trying to be a Christian.

Neither picture attacks the old thing. The garment is not condemned for being a garment; the skin was perfectly good in its day and did its job. They are simply asked to contain something they were never built to hold, and they fail. What Jesus has brought is not an improved version of what was there before. It is different in kind.

And the way most of us instinctively approach religion is patchwork. We take the life we have, with the self firmly in charge of it, and we sew something on: church on Sunday, a habit of prayer, a tidied-up vocabulary, a few things given up. The garment is the same garment. The patch is decoration.

This is why a certain kind of half-Christianity makes people more miserable than they were before, and why they are so often blamed for it unfairly. They are not lacking sincerity. They are living out exactly what Jesus describes: a new patch on an old coat, pulling at the seams every time life gets wet, producing a worse tear. Something in them keeps ripping, and they conclude that faith does not work, when what has failed is the repair job.

So test yours honestly. Is Christ an addition to your life — an important one, a costly one, but an addition to a self that still holds the deciding vote? Or has the self been handed over? The two look similar from outside for a long time and they behave completely differently under strain.

But new wine is for fresh wineskins. And there is the whole gospel in the last clause, which almost everybody reads past on the way out.

He does not leave you holding a jar of wine and a ruined skin, told to go and find a better container. He gives the skin. I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you; I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (Ezek. 36:26). If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation (2 Cor. 5:17). The making of a vessel that can hold what he pours is his work and not yours, which is exactly why it can be asked of you.

He did not come to mend you. Sit with that a moment, because it is worse news than you wanted and immeasurably better than you hoped. Mending would have left you with the old coat and the old rips and a lifetime of stitching. Instead he intends to make you new — and the wine he has to pour is so alive, so far beyond anything the old self could contain, that it would burst you as you are.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The field (vv. 23–24). The disciples walk through standing grain on a Sabbath, pulling heads off as they go and rubbing them in their hands. The Law explicitly allowed this; the Pharisees are not accusing them of theft. They are counting it as harvesting, threshing and winnowing — three of the thirty-nine categories of forbidden work, in one mouthful of wheat. And somebody had to be out in that field, on a Sabbath, watching.

The precedent (vv. 25–26). Jesus answers with a story rather than a ruling: David, hungry and on the run, eating the consecrated bread that only priests were permitted to eat, and Scripture recording not a word against him. The parallel is not simply that need outranks regulation. It is that a king travelling in rejection with his men has been here before.

The verdict (vv. 27–28). Two sentences that reset everything. The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath — the day is a gift, and they had turned it into a scoring system. And then: the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath. The Giver is standing in the cornfield being told off for letting hungry men eat.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath (v. 28) is a claim of breathtaking scope, and it is easy to miss how far it reaches. The Sabbath is not a national custom that a rabbi might reinterpret. It is stitched into the fabric of creation — God rested on the seventh day and made it holy before there was an Israel, a Sinai or a Jew (Gen. 2:2–3) — and it was afterwards written into the covenant by the finger of God (Exod. 20:8–11). To be lord of it is to be lord of the created order and of the covenant together.

And the day was always pointing past itself. Israel entered the land and never really entered the rest; centuries later Scripture can still say there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God (Heb. 4:9). Every seventh evening for fifteen hundred years the nation rehearsed a rest it did not yet possess.

Put Mark's two sentences side by side and see what has happened. The Sabbath was made for man — so it is a gift. And the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath — so the Giver is standing in the field. The rest the day rehearsed turns out not to be a square on a calendar but a Person, and he is the one being scolded. They were defending the gift against the Giver.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: hungry men pulling grain on a walk, and religious experts who had positioned themselves in a cornfield on a Sabbath in order to observe an infringement.

Now: the same instinct wherever the keeping of a form has become more important than the person the form was given to serve — the church where a visitor's clothes are noticed before his face is, the family where the standard is enforced and the child is not enjoyed. The institution that crushes the person it was designed to serve has inverted its own purpose, and it usually does so while feeling unusually devout.

The practical half of the day is worth taking as seriously as the doctrine of it. A modern reader does not break the Sabbath by working in a field; he breaks it by never stopping — by carrying the office in his pocket to bed. Stopping for a day feels like negligence, and it exposes precisely what a man believes about who is holding the world together. It keeps turning without you. That is the humiliation, and it is also the rest.

verseByVerse.quote: One Sabbath he was going through the grainfields, and as they made their way, his disciples began to pluck heads of grain. And the Pharisees were saying to him, "Look, why are they doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Get the picture right, because almost everybody reads this as a story about stealing and it is not.

The disciples are walking a path through standing grain — field boundaries were unfenced and paths ran between them — and as they go they pull off heads of wheat, rub them between their palms to loosen the husk, blow the chaff away, and eat the grain. It is what a hungry man does on a walk, and the Law of Moses expressly permitted it: If you go into your neighbour's standing grain, you may pluck the ears with your hand, but you shall not put a sickle to your neighbour's standing grain (Deut. 23:25). God had legislated for hungry travellers.

So notice what the Pharisees do not say. They do not accuse anyone of theft. Their objection is the day.

What is not lawful on the Sabbath. By the reckoning that had grown up around the fourth commandment, thirty-nine categories of work were forbidden, and the disciples had just contrived to touch three of them in a single mouthful. Pulling the head off was reaping. Rubbing it in the hands was threshing. Blowing away the husk was winnowing. A man could be a farm labourer for a whole harvest in the time it takes to eat a handful of wheat.

Now here is the detail Mark leaves lying on the ground for you to pick up. How did the Pharisees see it?

They were there. On a Sabbath morning, out along a path through the grainfields, at a carefully calculated distance from home so that they were not themselves exceeding the permitted Sabbath journey — in position, watching a group of working men to see whether any of them would put a hand out. That is not an accident of geography. Somebody planned that walk.

Look. The word is almost a shout. They have been waiting for this.

And it is worth sitting with, because the same energy is alive in every generation and it always dresses as faithfulness. It is possible to be scrupulously careful about a rule and hard as flint about a person; to notice, at a glance, everything that is out of place in somebody's life, and never once notice that he is hungry. These men looked at a group of tired men eating raw wheat on a walk and saw a violation. Their Scriptures had told them what to see: I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hos. 6:6).

Try it as a test, in the plainest terms. Think of the last time you were sharply critical of another Christian — how he brings up his children, how he spends, what he does with his Sundays. Did you know, at the time, what was actually going on in that house? Or were you standing at the edge of the field with a clear view of the rule and none at all of the man?

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Have you never read what David did, when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God, in the time of Abiathar the high priest, and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those who were with him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not answer with a ruling. He answers with a story, and the story is a deliberate choice.

What David did. The episode is 1 Samuel 21. David is already anointed king and is not yet on the throne; he is running from Saul with a few men, hungry, and he comes to the sanctuary at Nob. The only food in the place is the bread of the Presence — twelve loaves set out fresh before God every Sabbath, and the loaves taken away were to be eaten by the priests alone, a most holy portion (Lev. 24:5–9). The priest gives it to David and his men. And here is the thing Jesus expects them to have noticed: Scripture records not one syllable of criticism. God does not rebuke David, and the narrator does not either.

So the first point is the obvious one. Where a genuine human need collided with a cultic regulation, the regulation gave way and heaven did not object. The rule was never the ultimate thing.

But there is a second point in the choice of this story, and it is sharper. Jesus does not pick a case about hunger in general. He picks the anointed king — rejected, unrecognised, on the road, with his men — being fed from the holy table. The disciples in that grainfield are the men of a King the country has not enthroned, and if the men of David could eat the bread of the Presence because of who was with them, the Pharisees ought to be asking a much larger question than the one they came with.

A note on Abiathar. An honest reader with a reference Bible will notice something, and it is better dealt with plainly than hurried past: 1 Samuel 21 names the priest as Ahimelech, and Mark's Jesus says in the time of Abiathar the high priest. Abiathar was Ahimelech's son.

This is not a discovered embarrassment. It has been discussed openly in the church for many centuries, and there are two good answers.

The first is a matter of Greek. The phrase can as easily mean in the passage about Abiathar — exactly the construction Mark uses later when Jesus says have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush (12:26). The Hebrew Scriptures had no chapter numbers, so a teacher located a text by naming its most famous figure, and this stretch of 1 Samuel is Abiathar's section: he is the one who escapes the slaughter at Nob a chapter later and becomes David's priest for a lifetime. On that reading Jesus is giving a reference, not a date, and there is nothing to reconcile.

The second is simpler still. Abiathar was present at the sanctuary, and he, not his father, became the celebrated high priest of David's reign. Naming the era by its best-known man is how everybody talks about the past.

What matters for a reader who is not a specialist is this: nothing in the argument depends on it. Jesus is not resting his case on which priest was on duty. He is resting it on what God did not say when hungry men ate holy bread — and the Pharisees, who knew that chapter far better than we do, did not raise the objection. They had a much bigger problem coming in the next two verses.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two sentences, and between them they reset the entire subject.

The Sabbath was made for man. Mark's word is that it came into being for man — it was made, brought about, given. And it was given long before there was a Jew in the world to keep it. God rested on the seventh day and blessed it and made it holy on the last page of the creation account (Gen. 2:2–3), centuries before Sinai. This is not a piece of national religious custom. It is part of the architecture of the world, like marriage, like work, like day and night.

Which means it was a kindness. A day laid into the week when the ox is unhitched and the servant is off and the slave rests, when the poorest labourer in Israel gets what only rich men in the ancient world could buy — a day that is his. The Egyptians had given Israel no such day. God's first commandment about the seventh day is set out with the memory of slavery attached (Deut. 5:15).

Not man for the Sabbath. And there is the inversion. They had taken a day designed to lift a burden off a man's back and turned it into a burden to carry — a day with thirty-nine categories to be tracked, a day you could fail. The gift had become an examination.

So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath. Follow the logic and it is stunning. If the day was made for man, then the Man in whom humanity is summed up — the one Daniel saw given dominion — is its lord. He is not proposing a relaxation of the rules. He is telling a group of experts, in a cornfield, that the day belongs to him.

Now the question a reader who is not a scholar actually wants answered. Does this mean I have to keep a Sabbath? Is Sunday a rule?

Christians who love the Bible have not landed in the same place on this, and it is only fair to say so. Some hold that the fourth commandment, being rooted in creation and written into the Ten, still binds one day in seven, now observed on the day of the resurrection. Others read Paul's one person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike (Rom. 14:5) and let no one pass judgement on you... with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath (Col. 2:16), and hold that the shadow has been fulfilled in Christ and the day is now a matter of freedom.

But here is what neither side disputes, and it is the part that will actually change your week. The day is a gift and not a scoring system, and a man who never stops has not understood the God who did.

So make it concrete, because this is not a theory. Do you stop? Not slow down — stop. Is there a stretch of twenty-four hours in your week when the work is genuinely down, the phone is not being checked under the table, the inbox is not being glanced at from bed, and you are not quietly earning your right to exist? Most of us now break the Sabbath in a way the Pharisees would not have recognised: not by putting a hand to grain, but by never taking a hand off anything.

And be honest about why stopping is frightening. If you stop, things carry on without you. The work gets done or it does not; the world turns; you find out you were not holding it up. That is the humiliation in it, and it is also precisely the rest in it. It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep (Ps. 127:2). A day off is a weekly, physical confession that you are not God and are not needed to be.

Which is why it always pointed past itself. Israel came into the land and never came into the rest; the writer to the Hebrews, looking back over the whole story, says that there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God (Heb. 4:9). Every seventh evening for fifteen hundred years, a nation rehearsed something it did not yet have.

And then, on an ordinary Sabbath morning, in a wheat field in Galilee, the rest itself walked through the standing grain with a handful of hungry men — and was told off for it by the people who had spent their lives guarding the rehearsal. They were defending the gift against the Giver.

He is still the rest. Not a square on the calendar, not a scheme for the well-organised, but the one who says Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28) — and who gave it at the cost of a Friday on which he had no rest at all, so that the sleep of his beloved might be secured forever.

2.theology:
Chapter 2 opens the conflict that ends at the cross. The scribes and Pharisees are not villains in a simple morality tale — they are serious people defending serious religious commitments, and on the doctrine of forgiveness they are exactly right. Their error is not that they take the law too seriously; it is that they have not recognised the one the law was pointing to. When the fulfilment arrives, the categories built to anticipate it can no longer contain it, which is precisely the burden of the new wine and the old skins.

Four demonstrations, then, of why Jesus could not simply be absorbed into the religious system as constituted: he forgives sins directly rather than through the temple; he receives the excluded at his own table rather than at the end of a purification process; he calls his own presence a wedding rather than a fast; and he claims lordship over the creation ordinance of the Sabbath itself. Not because he is lawless, but because he is the law's Lord.
2.examples:
The Pharisees' discomfort at Jesus eating with sinners deserves sympathetic treatment before it receives critique. Their instinct toward purity was not irrational; it was a serious attempt to guard the holiness God had commanded, in a land under pagan occupation where the pressure to blur every line was constant. Their error was a category error: they had equated association with endorsement. Jesus's presence among sinners was not approval of their sin but the physician's presence among the sick, and the cure requires proximity. The model is the incarnation itself — the holy God does not deal with human ruin from a safe distance but comes into it to heal from within, and finally takes the disease into his own body on a cross.

Then: Pharisees keeping a careful distance in order to stay clean, while the one man in Capernaum who actually was clean reclined at a tax collector's table. Now: any form of Christianity that has quietly confused holiness with non-exposure — and, on the other side, any form of it that sits down at every table and never says who it came with.

3.title: By Whose Power?
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Again he entered the synagogue, and a man was there with a withered hand. <sup>2</sup>And they watched Jesus, to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him. <sup>3</sup>And he said to the man with the withered hand, “Come here.” <sup>4</sup>And he said to them, “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?” But they were silent. <sup>5</sup>And he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored. <sup>6</sup>The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him. <sup>7</sup>Jesus withdrew with his disciples to the sea, and a great crowd followed, from Galilee and Judea <sup>8</sup>and Jerusalem and Idumea and from beyond the Jordan and from around Tyre and Sidon. When the great crowd heard all that he was doing, they came to him. <sup>9</sup>And he told his disciples to have a boat ready for him because of the crowd, lest they crush him, <sup>10</sup>for he had healed many, so that all who had diseases pressed around him to touch him. <sup>11</sup>And whenever the unclean spirits saw him, they fell down before him and cried out, “You are the Son of God.” <sup>12</sup>And he strictly ordered them not to make him known. <sup>13</sup>And he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. <sup>14</sup>And he appointed twelve (whom he also named apostles) so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach <sup>15</sup>and have authority to cast out demons. <sup>16</sup>He appointed the twelve: Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter); <sup>17</sup>James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder); <sup>18</sup>Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Zealot, <sup>19</sup>and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. <sup>20</sup>Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. <sup>21</sup>And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, “He is out of his mind.” <sup>22</sup>And the scribes who came down from Jerusalem were saying, “He is possessed by Beelzebul,” and “by the prince of demons he casts out the demons.” <sup>23</sup>And he called them to him and said to them in parables, “How can Satan cast out Satan? <sup>24</sup>If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. <sup>25</sup>And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. <sup>26</sup>And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end. <sup>27</sup>But no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house. <sup>28</sup>“Truly, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter, <sup>29</sup>but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin”— <sup>30</sup>for they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.” <sup>31</sup>And his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent to him and called him. <sup>32</sup>And a crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him, “Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you.” <sup>33</sup>And he answered them, “Who are my mother and my brothers?” <sup>34</sup>And looking about at those who sat around him, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! <sup>35</sup>For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother.”
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is where the opposition hardens into a decision and the alternative community is formed. It opens with a trap in a synagogue and closes with a redefinition of family, and between the two everything about Jesus is contested. The Pharisees and Herodians — parties who agreed on nothing — walk out of a Sabbath service together to plan his death (v. 6). His own family concludes he is out of his mind and comes to take him home (v. 21). A delegation of scribes travels ninety miles from Jerusalem and pronounces him possessed (v. 22). Three verdicts, and all of them wrong.

Against that, Jesus does two constructive things. He appoints twelve men — a number no Jew could hear innocently — so that they might be with him and be sent out (vv. 13–15); and he tells the room what the kingdom actually is: a break-in. A stronger man has entered the strong man's house, tied him up, and is carrying out his property (v. 27). Every healing and deliverance in this Gospel is loot from that raid. The chapter ends by naming who now belongs to him, and the criterion is neither blood nor pedigree but doing the will of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Withered Hand and the Widening Response
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The trap (vv. 1–2). Jesus walks into a synagogue where two things are waiting for him: a man with a ruined hand, and a row of men watching to see whether he will touch it. Mark's word for their watching is the word for surveillance. They are not curious. They are collecting evidence.

The question nobody would answer (vv. 3–4). He puts the man in the middle of the room and asks whether the Sabbath is for doing good or doing harm, saving life or killing. It is unanswerable, and they know it, so they say nothing.

The anger (v. 5). The only place in Mark where we are told Jesus was angry — and in the same breath, grieved. Then a command to a man who cannot obey it, and a hand made new.

The verdict (v. 6). Two parties who despised each other walk out together to plan a murder, and it is still the Sabbath.

The crowds (vv. 7–12). He withdraws, and a hundred-mile radius follows him to the shore. He asks for a boat to keep from being crushed, and silences the only voices in the crowd that know exactly who he is.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verses 11–12 raise a question every attentive reader hits sooner or later: the demons keep saying true things about Jesus, and he keeps shutting them up. Why refuse free advertising from witnesses who cannot be wrong?

Two reasons converge, and the second is the one that touches the reader. The first is timing. In Galilee in that decade, to be publicly proclaimed Son of God meant one thing to a crowd — a nationalist king who would clear out the Romans. Jesus refuses to be crowned before he is crucified, because a title accepted on those terms would have to be unlearned at the cross. He will let the word be said out loud when it can be defined by his death (15:39, on the lips of the officer at the foot of it).

The second is more searching. What the unclean spirits say is doctrinally perfect. You are the Son of God is exactly right, and it saves them from nothing. James makes the point without flinching: you believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe — and shudder (Jas. 2:19). A creed can be entirely correct and entirely worthless. The spirits here fall down before him, which is more than the scribes did, and confess his identity, which is more than the disciples had managed — and they remain what they are. Right belief about Christ is not the same as belonging to him, and this chapter will end by saying who does belong.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man with a shrivelled hand told to stand up in the middle of a watched synagogue, before anything had been healed, in front of the men who had come to build a case.

Now: every act of obedience that makes a person visible and vulnerable before the outcome is assured — the first time you say in an office that you are a Christian; the apology you make with no guarantee it will be received; the sin confessed to one other believer when it could have stayed hidden for life. He was asked to be conspicuous first and healed second, and he had no way of knowing the order in advance.

And notice what the same scene did to the watchers. They had come to see whether a rule would be broken, and they saw a crippled man made whole, and it did not move them an inch. It is possible to sit in a room where God is plainly at work and be entirely occupied with whether it is being done properly.

verseByVerse.quote: Again he entered the synagogue, and a man was there with a withered hand. And they watched Jesus, to see whether he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark says again, and it is doing real work. The last time Jesus was in a synagogue on a Sabbath in this Gospel, a demon screamed and the whole town talked about it for weeks (1:21–28). He knows what happens when he walks into these buildings. He goes in anyway.

Picture the room. A Galilean synagogue was not large — stone benches around three or four walls, the congregation facing inward, everybody able to see everybody. There is no back row to hide in. That detail decides the whole scene, because a man is about to be told to stand up in the middle of it.

A man was there with a withered hand. The word suggests a hand that has dried up — atrophied, shrunken, the muscle wasted, whether from injury, disease or a stroke of palsy. Luke, who was a doctor, notices it was the right hand (Luke 6:6), which in a world of manual labour is the difference between a tradesman and a beggar. An early Christian writing outside the New Testament remembers him saying: I was a mason, earning my living with my hands; I beg you, Jesus, give me back my health, that I need not beg my bread in shame. Whether or not those were his words, they are certainly his situation.

He is not dying. Nobody could argue that this was an emergency that could not wait a day, and that is precisely why the Pharisees have kept him. A borderline case makes the better trap.

And they watched Jesus. The Greek verb is the one used for keeping something under observation — watching closely, watching sideways, the way you watch a man you have already decided about. Mark does not say they wondered whether he could do it. They had seen enough by chapter 3 to be in no doubt that he could. What they were watching for was whether he would.

So that they might accuse him. This is the language of the courtroom. They are not gathering understanding; they are gathering evidence, and they have brought a man's disability into a religious service and used it as bait.

Stop there for a moment, because it is uglier than a quick reading allows. There is a human being in that room with a wasted hand and a wrecked livelihood, and the most religious men present have looked at him and seen an opportunity. He is not a person to them. He is a test case.

And that is what happens to religion when it detaches from love. Not usually in some dramatic collapse into wickedness — these men would have been horrified to be called wicked — but by degrees, until a suffering man in your own congregation registers primarily as an issue to be handled. If you have ever found yourself more interested in whether something was done correctly than in the person it was done to, you have felt the pull of that room.

Then hold the two halves of the verse together, because Mark has set them side by side deliberately. A man with a withered hand, and men with withered hearts. Only one of them knew he needed healing.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the man with the withered hand, "Come here." And he said to them, "Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?" But they were silent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not do this quietly. He could have. The man could have been healed on his way out, at the door, with nobody the wiser, and the trap would have closed on nothing. Instead: Come here. Some translations catch the force of it — stand up, into the middle, where the room can see you.

Everything about that is deliberate. If the healing is going to be treated as a crime, it will be committed in open court. Jesus is not caught breaking the Sabbath; he chooses the moment, the venue and the audience, and he makes the question unavoidable.

And spare a thought for the man, who has not asked for any of this. He did not come to the synagogue to be a test case. He came, presumably, as he had come for years, and hidden the hand inside his cloak the way you do. Now he is standing in the middle of the floor with the bad hand on display, in front of neighbours who have known about it all his life and religious officials who are visibly hostile — and nothing has happened yet. He is exposed first and healed second, and at this point in the story he has no way of knowing that the second part is coming.

Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill? Now watch what the question does, because it is not the question they were expecting.

They were braced for an argument about the category of work — whether healing counts, whether the case is urgent, which precedents apply. Jesus refuses the whole frame. He does not ask whether healing is permitted. He asks what the day is for.

And he leaves no third option. On any given Sabbath you are either doing good or doing harm; you are either saving life or destroying it. Neutrality is not one of the available positions, because to have the power to do good and to withhold it is itself a choice. James says it plainly: whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin (Jas. 4:17).

Then notice the second half of the question, because it is a blade. To save life or to kill. Who is killing anybody? Nobody, yet — but by the end of verse 6, the men in that room will have spent the Sabbath planning a death. Jesus has read what is in them, and he says it out loud before they have said it to each other. The Sabbath in which he restores a hand is the Sabbath in which they begin to plot a murder, and only one of those is work.

But they were silent. The silence is not ignorance. These men could argue any point of law in the Torah for an afternoon. They are silent because the question has only one honest answer and that answer costs them the case.

That kind of silence is worth recognising, because most of us have used it. It is the silence in which you do not deny what has just been said, and do not act on it either. It feels safer than being wrong. It is not. A man who says nothing has not stayed neutral; he has decided, and simply avoided the cost of saying so out loud. Six verses later that same silence walks out of the building and starts making arrangements.

verseByVerse.quote: And he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart, and said to the man, "Stretch out your hand." He stretched it out, and his hand was restored.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark now tells us something the other Gospels leave out, and it is the only place in this Gospel where we are told in plain words how Jesus felt about a group of people.

He looked around at them with anger. Not a glance. He swept the room, face by face, and what was in his own face was anger. Matthew and Luke both record the healing and both omit this; Mark, whose Gospel carries Peter's memory, keeps it, because Peter was standing there and saw it.

This needs saying carefully, because a great many people carry a picture of Jesus in which this verse cannot fit — endlessly mild, never provoked, incapable of a hard look. That picture is not from the Bible. The Jesus of the Gospels was angry here, made a whip and cleared the temple courts (John 2:15), and called men whitewashed tombs to their faces (Matt. 23:27). And he never sinned once.

So it is possible to be angry and holy at the same time. Be angry and do not sin (Eph. 4:26) is not a contradiction; it is a command with a boundary. Which raises the practical question: how do you tell the two apart?

Mark answers it in the same sentence, and the answer is the second word.

Grieved at their hardness of heart. The anger and the grief are one motion. He is not merely furious; he is cut to the heart over what these men have become. The Greek word behind hardness is the word for a callus, or for the way a broken bone heals over into something stony — tissue that was once soft, thickening at the very point of injury until it can no longer feel.

And there is your test, and it is the one that will do you good this week. Sinful anger enjoys itself. It wants the other person diminished; it rehearses the argument in the shower; it would be quietly disappointed if they repented, because then there would be nothing to be right about. Righteous anger grieves. It hurts to feel it. It wants the wrong put right and the wrongdoer restored, and it would be delighted to be made unnecessary.

Run that on the last thing you were angry about. Did you want the person changed, or did you want them beaten? You will know the answer in about four seconds, and it is worth knowing.

Stretch out your hand. And now the command, which is impossible. That is the whole point of it. This is exactly the thing the man cannot do; if he could stretch out that hand he would not have spent his life hiding it in his cloak. He has almost certainly tried a thousand times.

He stretched it out, and his hand was restored. Mark gives no interval. There is no description of warmth spreading, no gradual return of movement. He obeyed, and in the obeying the power was there.

Do not miss the order, because it is the order of the Christian life. He does not stretch out a hand that has been healed. The stretching is where the healing happens. Faith is not the feeling of confidence you wait to receive before you move; faith is moving on his word while you still feel exactly as incapable as you did a minute ago.

Which is the answer to a question a lot of believers are quietly stuck on: I would obey if I had more faith. No. You will find you had the faith in the doing of it. Make the phone call. Say the sentence. Open the Bible at six in the morning when nothing in you wants to. The strength arrives in the stretching and never before it.

And look, last, at what those two hands mean together. One hand withered and useless, held out at his command and made new. And his own hands — sound, strong, a workman's hands — stretched out one Friday on a piece of wood and ruined, so that the ruined might be restored. He healed with a word what would cost him nails.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees went out and immediately held counsel with the Herodians against him, how to destroy him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the verse slowly, because four things in it are worse than they look.

The Pharisees went out. They leave the building. There has just been an undeniable miracle in front of them, in a room they know, done to a man they have seen every week for years, and their response is to walk out of the service. Nothing is said about the hand. Nobody congratulates the man.

Immediately. Mark's word again. There is no interval of reflection, no going home to think and pray about it. The decision is made on the spot.

Held counsel with the Herodians. This is the detail a first-century reader would have found almost unbelievable, and it needs explaining because we no longer feel it.

The Pharisees were the strict separatists — men whose entire programme was the purity of Israel, who regarded collaboration with Rome as a filthy compromise and Herod's family as half-Edomite puppets propped up by pagan soldiers.
